parsed.canonical_question: How much ATP does glycolysis produce and how does it feed the mitochondrion?

rendering.title: Glycolysis ATP yield and pyruvate entry into the mitochondrion
rendering.explanation:
Glycolysis is the first stage of cellular respiration and takes place in the cytoplasm. Starting from one molecule of glucose (a 6-carbon sugar), glycolysis produces two 3-carbon molecules called pyruvate.

In terms of ATP, glycolysis has two phases. The investment phase uses 2 ATP to activate glucose. The payoff phase regenerates 4 ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation. The net yield is therefore 2 ATP per glucose. The pathway also reduces 2 NAD+ to 2 NADH, which will later donate their electrons to the electron transport chain.

Pyruvate cannot diffuse freely across the inner mitochondrial membrane. It is transported into the mitochondrial matrix by the mitochondrial pyruvate carrier (MPC), a protein complex embedded in the inner membrane. Once inside the matrix, pyruvate is converted into acetyl-CoA by the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex. This step releases one molecule of carbon dioxide per pyruvate and produces one NADH. The resulting acetyl-CoA then enters the Krebs cycle.

So glycolysis feeds the mitochondrion in two ways: it supplies pyruvate (converted to acetyl-CoA for the Krebs cycle) and cytoplasmic NADH (whose electrons are shuttled into the matrix by carrier systems such as the malate-aspartate shuttle).
summary_bullets: Glycolysis converts one glucose into two pyruvate molecules in the cytoplasm.
The net ATP yield from glycolysis is 2 ATP per glucose (4 produced minus 2 invested).
Glycolysis also produces 2 NADH, which carry electrons for the electron transport chain.
Pyruvate crosses the inner mitochondrial membrane via the mitochondrial pyruvate carrier (MPC).
In the matrix, pyruvate dehydrogenase converts pyruvate into acetyl-CoA, CO2, and NADH.
Acetyl-CoA then enters the Krebs cycle to continue energy extraction.
